entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Job.39.5-Job.8.5">Job 39:5-8   5</reference>  Who hath sent forth the wild ass free, <div eID="gen8662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8663" type="x-p"/> And who loosed the bands of the wild ass,   6  Whose house I made the steppe, <div eID="gen8663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8664" type="x-p"/> And his dwelling the salt country?   7  He scorneth the tumult of the city, <div eID="gen8664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8665" type="x-p"/> He heareth not the noise of the driver.   8  That which is seen upon the mountains is his pasture, <div eID="gen8665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8666" type="x-p"/> And he sniffeth after every green thing. <div eID="gen8666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8667" type="x-p"/> On the wild ass (not: ass of the forest).<note placement="foot">It is a dirty yellow with a white belly, single-hoofed and long-eared; its hornless head somewhat resembles that of the gazelle, but is much later; its hair has the dryness of the hair of the deer, and the animal forms the transition from the stag and deer genus to the ass. It is entirely distinct from the mahâ or baqar el-wahsh, wild ox, whose large soft eyes are so much celebrated by the poets of the steppe. This latter is horned and double-hoofed, and forms the transition from the stag to the ox distinct from the <hi type="italic">ri'm</hi>, ראם, therefore perhaps an antelope of the kind of the Indian <hi type="italic">nîlgau</hi>, blue ox, <hi type="italic">Portax tragocamelus</hi>. I have not seen both kinds of animals alive, but I have often seen their skins in the tents of the <hi type="italic">Ruwalâ</hi>. Both kinds are remarkable for their very swift running, and it is especially affirmed of the <hi type="italic">ferâ</hi> that no rider can overtake it. In spite of its difficulty and hazardousness, the nomads are passionately given to hunting the wild ass, and the proverb cited by the Kâmûs: <hi type="italic">kull es - sêd bigôf el - ferâ</hi> (every hunt sticks in the belly of the <hi type="italic">ferâ</hi>, i.e., compared with that, every other hunt is nothing), is perfectly correct. When the approach of a herd, which always consists of several hundred, is betrayed by a cloud of dust which can be seen many miles off, so many horsemen rise up from all sides in pursuit that the animals are usually scattered, and single ones are obtained by the dogs and by shots. Parallel with ערבה (according to its etymon perhaps, land of darkness, <hi type="italic">terra incognita</hi>) is מלחה, salt <hi type="italic">adj</hi>. or (sc. ארץ) a salt land, i.e., therefore unfruitful and incapable of culture, as the country round the Salt Sea of Palestine: that the wild ass even gladly licks the salt or natron of the desert, is a matter of fact, and may be assumed, since all wild animals that feed on plants have a partiality, which is based on chemical laws of life, for licking slat. S. 419, Anm.). entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Job.39.9-Job.12.9">Job 39:9-12   9</reference>  Will the oryx be willing to serve thee, <div eID="gen8668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8669" type="x-p"/> Or will he lodge in thy crib? 10  Canst thou bind the oryx in the furrow with a leading rein, <div eID="gen8669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8670" type="x-p"/> Or will he harrow the valleys, following thee? 11  Wilt thou trust him because his strength is great, <div eID="gen8670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8671" type="x-p"/> And leave thy labour to him? 12  Wilt thou confide in him to bring in thy sowing, <div eID="gen8671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8672" type="x-p"/> And to garner thy threshing-floor? <div eID="gen8672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8673" type="x-p"/> In correct texts רים has a <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi> in the <hi type="italic">Resh</hi>, and היאבה the accent on the <hi type="italic">penult.,</hi> as <reference osisRef="Prov.11.21">Pro 11:21</reference> ינּקה רע, and <reference osisRef="Jer.39.12">Jer 39:12</reference> רּע מאוּמה. The tone retreats according to the rule, Ges. §29, 3, <hi type="italic">b</hi>; and the <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi> is, as also when the second word begins with an aspirate,<note placement="foot">The National Grammarians call this exception to the rule, that the <hi type="italic">muta</hi> is aspirated when the preceding word ends with a vowel, אתי מרחיק (<hi type="italic">veniens e longinquo</hi>), i.e., the case, where the word ending with a vowel is <hi type="italic">Milel</hi>, whether from the very first, or, when the second word is a monosyllable or has the tone on the <hi type="italic">penult.,</hi> on account of the accent that has retreated (in order to avoid two syllables with the chief tone coming together); in this case the aspirate, and in general the initial letter (if capable of being doubled) of the second monosyllabic or <hi type="italic">penultima</hi>-accented word, takes a <hi type="italic">Dagesh;</hi> but this is not without exceptions that are quite as regular. The Chethib here uses the Kal שׁוּב transitively: to bring back (viz., that which was sown as harvested), which is possible (vid., Job 42:10 ). גרנך, Job 39:12 , is either a locative (into thy threshing-floor) or acc . of the obj. per synecd. continentis pro contento, as Rth 3:2; Mat 3:12. entries.content_osis: Job 39:19-25 19  Dost thou give to the horse strength? <div eID="gen8685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8688" type="x-p"/> Dost thou clothe his neck with flowing hair? 20  Dost thou cause him to leap about like the grasshopper? <div eID="gen8688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8689" type="x-p"/> The noise of his snorting is a terror! 21  He paweth the ground in the plain, and boundeth about with strength. <div eID="gen8689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8690" type="x-p"/> He advanceth to meet an armed host. 22  He laugheth at fear, and is not affrighted, <div eID="gen8690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8691" type="x-p"/> And turneth not back from the sword. 23  The quiver rattleth over him, <div eID="gen8691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8692" type="x-p"/> The glittering lance and spear. 24  With fierceness and rage he swalloweth the ground, <div eID="gen8692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8693" type="x-p"/> And standeth not still, when the trumpet soundeth. 25  He saith at every blast of the trumpet: Ha, ha! <div eID="gen8693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8694" type="x-p"/> And from afar he scenteth the battle, <div eID="gen8694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8695" type="x-p"/> The thundering of the captains and the shout of war. <div eID="gen8695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8696" type="x-p"/> After the ostrich, which, as the Arabs say, is composed of the nature of a bird and a camel, comes the horse in its heroic beauty, and impetuous lust for the battle, which is likewise an evidence of the wisdom of the Ruler of the world - a wisdom which demands the admiration of men. This passage of the book of Job, says K. Löffler, in his <hi type="italic">Gesch. des Pferdes </hi>(1863), is the oldest and most beautiful description of the horse. It may be compared to the praise of the horse in Hammer-Purgstall’s <hi type="italic">Duftkörner;</hi> it deserves more than this latter the praise of majestic simplicity, which is the first feature of classic superiority. Jer. falsely renders <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.39.19">Job 39:19</reference></hi>: <hi type="italic">aut circumdabis collo ejus hinnitum;</hi> as Schlottm., who also wishes to be so understood: Dost thou adorn his neck with the voice of thunder? The neck (צוּאר, prop. the twister, as Persic <hi type="italic">gerdân , gerdan ,</hi> from צוּר, Arab. <hi type="italic">ṣâr</hi>, to twist by pressure, to turn, bend, as Pers. from <hi type="italic">gerdı̂den</hi>, to turn one’s self, twist) has nothing to do with the voice of neighing. But רעמה also does not signify dignity (Ew. 113, <hi type="italic">d</hi>), but the mane, and is not from רעם = ראם = רם, the hair of the mane, as being above, like λοφιά, but from רעם, <hi type="italic">tremere</hi>, the mane as quivering, trembling (Eliz. Smith: the shaking mane); like φόβη, according to Kuhn, cogn. with σόβη, the tail, from φοβεῖν (σοβεῖν), to wag, shake, scare, comp. άΐ́σσεσθαι of the mane, <hi type="italic">Il</hi>. vi. 510.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Job.39.26-Job.30.26">Job 39:26-30 26</reference>  Doth the hawk fly by thy wisdom, <div eID="gen8698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8699" type="x-p"/> Doth it spread its wings towards the south? 27  Or is it at thy command that the eagle soareth aloft, <div eID="gen8699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8700" type="x-p"/> And buildeth its nest on high? 28  It inhabiteth the rock, and buildeth its nest <div eID="gen8700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8701" type="x-p"/> Upon the crag of the rock and fastness. 29  From thence it seeketh food, <div eID="gen8701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8702" type="x-p"/> Its eyes see afar off. 30  And its young ones suck up blood; <div eID="gen8702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8703" type="x-p"/> And where the slain are, there is it. <div eID="gen8703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8704" type="x-p"/> The ancient versions are unanimous in testifying that, according to the signification of the root, נץ signifies the hawk (which is significant in the Hieroglyphics): the soaring one, the high-flyer (comp. Arab. <hi type="italic">nṣṣ</hi>, to rise, struggle forwards, and Arab. <hi type="italic">nḍḍ</hi>, to raise the wings for flight). The <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. יאבר- (jussive form in the question, as <reference osisRef="Job.13.27">Job 13:27</reference>) might signify: to get feathers, <hi type="italic">plumescere</hi> (Targ., Jer.), but that gives a tame question; wherefore Gregory understands the <hi type="italic">plumescit</hi> of the Vulgate of moulting, for which purpose the hawk seeks the sunny side. But האביר alone, by itself, cannot signify “to get new feathers;” moreover, an annual moulting is common to all birds, and prominence is alone given to the new feathering of the eagle in the Old Testament, <reference osisRef="Ps.103.5">Psa 103:5</reference>; Mic 1:16, comp. <reference osisRef="Isa.40.31">Isa 40:31</reference> (lxx πτεροφυήσουσιν ὡς ἀετοί).<note placement="foot">Less unfavourable to this rendering is the following, that אברה signifies the long feathers, and אבר the wing that is composed of them (perhaps, since the Talm. אברים signifies wings and limbs, <hi type="italic">artus</hi>, from אבר = הבר, Arab. <hi type="italic">hbr</hi>, to divide, furnish with joints), although נוצה (from נצה, to fly) is the more general designation of the feathers of birds.</note> <div eID="gen8704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8705" type="x-p"/> Thus, then, the point of the question will lie in לתימן: the hawk is a bird of passage, God has endowed it with instinct to migrate to the south as the winter season is approaching. <div eID="gen8705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8706" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Job.39.27">Job 39:27</reference> the circle of the native figures taken from animal life, which began with the lion, the king of quadrupeds, is now closed with the eagle, the king of birds. It is called נשׁר, from נשׁר, Arab. <hi type="italic">nsr , vellere;</hi> as also <hi type="italic">vultur</hi> (by virtue of a strong power of assimilation = <hi type="italic">vultor</hi>) is derived from <hi type="italic">vellere</hi>, - a common name of the golden eagle, the lamb’s vulture, the carrion-kite (<hi type="italic">Cathartes percnopterus</hi>), and indeed also of other kinds of kites and falcons. There is nothing to prevent our understanding the eagle κατ ̓ εξοχήν, viz., the golden eagle (<hi type="italic">Aquila chrysaëtos</hi>), in the present passage; for even to this, corpses, though not already putrified, are a welcome prey. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.39.27">Job 39:27</reference></hi> we must translate either: and is it at thy command that ... ? or: is it so that (as in הכי) at thy command ... ? The former is more natural here. מצוּדה, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.39.28">Job 39:28</reference></hi>, signifies prop. <hi type="italic">specula</hi> (from צוּד, to spy); then, however, as Arab. <hi type="italic">masâd</hi> (referred by the original lexicons to <hi type="italic">masada</hi>), the high hill, and the mountain-top. The rare form יעלעוּ, for which Ges., Olsh., and others wish to read לעלעוּ or ילעלעוּ (from לוּע, <hi type="italic">deglutire</hi>), is to be derived from עלע, a likewise secondary form out of עלעל (from עוּל, to suck, to give suck), (Note: The Arab. <hi type="italic">‛alla</hi> does not belong here: it gains the signification <hi type="italic">iterum bibere</hi> from the primary signification of “coming over or upon anything,” which branches out in various ways: to take a second, third, etc., drink after the first. More on this point on Isa 3:4. <div eID="gen8706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8707" type="x-p"/> Supplementary note: The quadriliteral עלעל to be supposed, is not to be derived from עלל, and is not, as it recently has been, to be compared with Arab. <hi type="italic">‛ll ,</hi> “to drink.” This Arab. verb does not signify “to drink” at all, but, among many other branchings out of its general primary signification, related to עלה, Arab. <hi type="italic">‛lâ</hi>, also signifies: “to take a second, third, etc., drink after the first,” concerning which more details will be given elsewhere. עלעל goes back to עוּל, <hi type="italic">lactare</hi>, with the middle vowel, whence also עויל, <reference osisRef="Job.16.11">Job 16:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.12.18">Job 12:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.21.11">Job 21:11</reference> (which see). entries.content_plain: Job 39:26-30 26 Doth the hawk fly by thy wisdom, Doth it spread its wings towards the south? 27 Or is it at thy command that the eagle soareth aloft, And buildeth its nest on high? 28 It inhabiteth the rock, and buildeth its nest Upon the crag of the rock and fastness. 29 From thence it seeketh food, Its eyes see afar off. 30 And its young ones suck up blood; And where the slain are, there is it. The ancient versions are unanimous in testifying that, according to the signification of the root, נץ signifies the hawk (which is significant in the Hieroglyphics): the soaring one, the high-flyer (comp. Arab. nṣṣ , to rise, struggle forwards, and Arab. nḍḍ , to raise the wings for flight). The Hiph . יאבר- (jussive form in the question, as Job 13:27 ) might signify: to get feathers, plumescere (Targ., Jer.), but that gives a tame question; wherefore Gregory understands the plumescit of the Vulgate of moulting, for which purpose the hawk seeks the sunny side. But האביר alone, by itself, cannot signify “to get new feathers;” moreover, an annual moulting is common to all birds, and prominence is alone given to the new feathering of the eagle in the Old Testament, Psa 103:5 ; Mic 1:16, comp. Isa 40:31 (lxx πτεροφυήσουσιν ὡς ἀετοί). Less unfavourable to this rendering is the following, that אברה signifies the long feathers, and אבר the wing that is composed of them (perhaps, since the Talm. אברים signifies wings and limbs, artus , from אבר = הבר, Arab. hbr , to divide, furnish with joints), although נוצה (from נצה, to fly) is the more general designation of the feathers of birds. Thus, then, the point of the question will lie in לתימן: the hawk is a bird of passage, God has endowed it with instinct to migrate to the south as the winter season is approaching. In Job 39:27 the circle of the native figures taken from animal life, which began with the lion, the king of quadrupeds, is now closed with the eagle, the king of birds. It is called נשׁר, from נשׁר, Arab. nsr , vellere; as also vultur (by virtue of a strong power of assimilation = vultor ) is derived from vellere , - a common name of the golden eagle, the lamb’s vulture, the carrion-kite ( Cathartes percnopterus ), and indeed also of other kinds of kites and falcons. There is nothing to prevent our understanding the eagle κατ ̓ εξοχήν, viz., the golden eagle ( Aquila chrysaëtos ), in the present passage; for even to this, corpses, though not already putrified, are a welcome prey. In Job 39:27 we must translate either: and is it at thy command that ... ? or: is it so that (as in הכי) at thy command ... ? The former is more natural here. מצוּדה, Job 39:28 , signifies prop. specula (from צוּד, to spy); then, however, as Arab. masâd (referred by the original lexicons to masada ), the high hill, and the mountain-top. The rare form יעלעוּ, for which Ges., Olsh., and others wish to read לעלעוּ or ילעלעוּ (from לוּע, deglutire ), is to be derived from עלע, a likewise secondary form out of עלעל (from עוּל, to suck, to give suck), (Note: The Arab. ‛alla does not belong here: it gains the signification iterum bibere from the primary signification of “coming over or upon anything,” which branches out in various ways: to take a second, third, etc., drink after the first. More on this point on Isa 3:4. Fürst, Handwörterbuch, sub עוּל, since instances are wanting in favour of עלע being formed out of לעלע ( Jesurun , p. 164). Schult. not inappropriately compares even גלג = גלגל in גּלגּתא, Γολγοθᾶ = גּלגּלתּא. The concluding words, Job 39:30 , are perhaps echoed in Mat 24:28. High up on a mountain-peak the eagle builds its eyrie, and God has given it a remarkably sharp vision, to see far into the depth below the food that is there for it and its young ones. Not merely from the valley in the neighbourhood of its eyrie, but often from distant plains, which lie deep below on the other side of the mountain range, it seizes its prey, and rises with it even to the clouds, and bears it home to its nest. Vid., the beautiful description in Charles Boner’s Forest Creatures , 1861. Thus does God work exceeding strangely, but wonderously, apparently by contradictions, but in truth most harmoniously and wisely, in the natural world.
